questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: When I was choosing between destinations, the most important aspect for me was that I could be a place where I felt I would love the environment and the University was well known. When choosing I was between either the US and the UK, but ultimately decided the UK as both have common law, and also being a bit closer to the European legal market.  University of Nottingham has an amazing campus and sports facilities, and there are green spaces everywhere. It was also "easy" to find accommodation through the University although a bit expensive and troublesome if you become a graduate student.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My overall experience in Nottingham was great. I made some great friends, had some exciting courses, and Nottingham was close to a bunch of really nice cities in the UK. I however have had quite a bit of trouble with the accommodation team of University of Nottingham, and would recommend any other student to not find housing through the University if they are 1) Upgraded to graduate student or 2) Plan to leave before the end-date of the semester.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: When I arrived it was somewhat easy to find the information I needed to know upon arrival. I quickly figured out I had to get my student card from the Students Union (and not the security office).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not receive and assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I had been promised someone would be ready to welcome me even though my flight and bus to University of Nottingham (UoN) was to arrive quite late. However, when I arrived there were no-one there to help me, and I instead was lucky to find some staff that was walking around so I could get my room. When you arrive in the Spring semester there is not really a orientation week, rather you meet some of the other students when the tutor (the official you speak to from Nottingham) hosts some gatherings for the exchange students.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: If you chose to get housing through the university you could choose between catered on-campus or non-catered off-campus. I imagine you could also try and find some outside of the university, as one of my friends found an AirBnB and lived there for some months. You can choose rooms that are ensuite or where you share bathrooms.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I lived on-campus in a catered hall (Ancaster Hall), and when you live catered you get the food made for you. However, the food that I had in the hall was very, very bad, often lacked any effort, and seemed very unhealthy. I know and tried some of the halls (like Cripps Hall and Lincoln Hall) where the food is better, but these are the only two where the food is somewhat better. Based on the food alone I would not recommend anyone to live catered, as the money you would save from living catered and not having to buy food simply is not worth it. Especially during the Easter break there was bad food.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
If the student decides to live in accommodation provided by the university, I would with everything I have recommend them NOT to live in a catered hall - Ancaster or Cripps or any other. While it was nice to live on-campus and be close, it simply was not worth it. People are generally also younger, so you tend to have firealarms go off at night for everyone a couple times a week, and this frustrates anyone. Please, do not choose catered. 
I have however heard quite well from people that lived at Broadgate Park or any of the other self-catered halls. It was my impression that these were quite a bit better, and you could make some great friends while still being quite close to the university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I have given the grade 2 because of the location of my room was great; It was on campus and I had a view out to some green grass. Everything else however was really bad. From the food as stated above to the firealarms at all times and very thin walls. As I was upgraded to postgraduate courses my semester ended around a month before what it normally would (in May), and I therefore from early April tried to resign from my room. This was however not possible, but would have been possible had I been informed there was a blanket that could have been signed. Instead I was told there was no way you would be able to resign your contract. This if of course something I have complained to the accommodation team. When talking with these I have a sense that it is not very organised; I met for a meeting where an employee to me that mistakes had happened from their office, but later when I made a formal complaint was given a very short denial with no real explanation and where it seemed nothing was read. While I have appealed this, the point is; The accommodation is okay if you choose self-catered and you are SURE you are not doing graduate level courses AND plan to stay until the official end-date, but bad in the case you i.e. get graduate level courses and want to leave a bit earlier, as your studies also have a end date sooner.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Registrering for courses was easy, and if you ask the conveyor of the course you might be allowed to do graduate level courses. However, some criminal law classes based on common-law (when it is graduate level) can be hard to get into (I was not allowed to have advanced criminal evidence as I had not had criminal evidence before).

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The first weeks you are able to participate and try the classes you can sign up for. I would recommend going to those you are interested in, and then later decide. UCPH was also great and amazing when it came to approval of courses. If I remember correctly you just sign into your Nottingham account and then sign up for the classes (or you can write and get help from academic affairs which I got).

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: As stated above, you could get help from academic affairs if you had trouble signing up for a class. I suppose you could also ask the professor running the class about what the class is about.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful, as I did not experience any problems (except the class where I did not have the proper prerequisites).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It is rather easy, and do not worry about it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic programme was rather nice, and I did like it. The classes were very different from each other, and it seemed that they were mostly discussion based.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of courses I had were graduate level courses (as I got approval). I would say they are quite a bit easier than those of Danish Law Master Courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Some of the teaching was quite different while some was the same. I.e. Criminal Justice was very much only focused on discussion and you would sit in a horse shoe-formation, and there would not really be a plan for the class other than the theme and some readings. IP Law classes were however more like just the professor speaking and not seeking that much input.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: 1. International and Comparative Patent Law, 2. International and Comparative Trade Mark Law, 3. Fair Trials, Human Rights and Criminal Justice, and 4. Global Competition Law and International Business

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend the criminal justice class if you are interested in criminal law. I really liked the teaching where you discussed a  lot, and I was also a huge fan of the topics. It gave me quite a bit of insights even though the professor is rather special and takes some time to adjust to. 
IP law classes were also good, however the professor I would say was very experienced and noted IP-law professor, but maybe did not prepare that much for class (instead relying on memory). Competition law was an amazing professor, but I was not that interested in the topic after having it some times.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It is a little difficult for me to write what unexpected costs were; I tried living rather cheap while being in the UK. Unexpected costs were more those were you decide to travel around the UK or decide to go to concerts and such. I feel Nottingham can be quite cheap if you get accommodation that is cheap (possible self-catered) and do not do that much. It all depends on how much you want to do.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Flying was less expensive that I imagined when travelling around the UK, Uber was not that expensive when travelling. While I did know the price of my housing, it was most definitely still very expensive. Alcohol was around the same price as in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The sports center of University of Nottingham is amazing and has great facilities. If you like bouldering / climbing it is quite nice.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were some social activities, but I would say you should go find them yourself.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go see some concerts as there are a lot fo well-known artists. I went to Sam Smith and Eden, but know Maroon 5 was there too. I would also recommend going to Ye Olde Jerusalem (supposedly the oldest pub in England). It is built inside a cave and looks cool. Also go see the Nottingham Castle and the Criminal Justice Museum.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Except travelling all over the UK, I would recommend further students to go to the city right by "Beeston". It seems very chill and, while some say it can be a bit unsafe at night, I never had any bad experiences there. They are a Tesco Express, some nice places to eat, and some cool rurals.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: English culture is very much like Danish culture. I would however say to bring your physical ID / Passport when going out and getting alcohol, as they do not accept the digital ones like they do in Denmark and they HAVE to check if they think you are under 25 (you still only need to be 18 to drink however(.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: When there is a zoom meeting at the start of the semester for incoming exchange students, go and see if you can find them on instagram or somewhere else and then meet up. Try and socialise as much as possible. You will als get a student tutor who will and can introduce you England / Campus life (but these vary on how active they are).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There were not really any. When you go and party people are a bit more rude (and drunk) than they are in Denmark. In the UK they also party every Wednesday instead of the weekends usually (you can still find large parties on Fridays though - not so much on Saturdays from my experience).

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciated the way you get to learn a lot more English, especially law English. The culture is again very much like Denmark, but being able to go to pubs and drink for quite cheap is rather nice. I did not appreciate the bad coffee though...

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1. Know if you want to go for graduate courses before going and make your accommodation decision based on that. If you get them, do you want to stay the whole trip, or (usually) end a month before and not do anything while having a room? 2. Do not live catered. I remember previous exchange students from DK that went to UoN all recommended me to live off-campus / self-catered, but I did not listen as I thought it would be interesting to have the "UK experience". It is however very difficult and annoying to live with fire alarms going off every day. 3. Remember to see all that the UK has to offer. The nature is quite beautiful; go and see Manchester and try and take the train ride there. You will see some amazing hills on that trip. Also go see Ireland if you can or Scotland; I went to Dublin which was okay, but Northern Ireland, Belfast, (part of UK) was such a pretty city.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The exchange is usually 5 months so you will not have difficulties with visa. You can however not work AT ALL while being there which is not so nice if you would want that. You also do have quite a bit of time off during the semester, as you have 3/4 weeks off during Easter Break, and then only one week of classes after.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Learning that I am able to live in a foreign country by myself. I have considering doing an LLM in a foreign country, so now I know I am able to live away from family.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It is of course very hard not seeing your family and friends, but from my experience it becomes completely okay as you make some new and really good friends. Exchange friends are just like you, and they also are looking for other people to talk with.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
